= BITwiki Evidence Framework =

'''How We Evaluate Evidence'''

----
== Purpose ==

This framework establishes how BITwiki evaluates evidence. Evidence has no fixed value—its utility depends on context. The framework provides systematic criteria for assessing evidentiary quality while rejecting rigid hierarchies that fail to account for domain-specific considerations and contextual dependencies.

The approach integrates insights from philosophy of science (Longino, 1990; Douglas, 2009), evidence-based practice (Sackett et al., 1996), and critical information studies (Fallis, 2008). By emphasizing context-dependency, we acknowledge that evidence quality cannot be determined through universal metrics but requires situated judgment.

----
== Core Principle: Context Matters ==

Evidence derives value from context, not from intrinsic properties.

'' A peer-reviewed article may be flawed by funding bias
'' An informal technical discussion may contain more insight than formal publications
'' Blockchain data is valuable for blockchain analysis, irrelevant for biology

We reject:
'' Fixed evidence hierarchies
'' Universal weights regardless of domain
'' Truth by consensus
'' Numeric scoring systems

=== The Context-Dependency Thesis ===

The value of evidence is fundamentally relational—it depends on the specific question being asked, the domain of inquiry, the available alternatives, and the purposes for which the evidence is being used. This thesis challenges traditional evidence hierarchies that attempt to rank evidence types independently of context (Howick, 2011).

----
== Evaluation Dimensions ==

When assessing evidence, consider:

| Dimension | Question |
|-----------|----------|
| '''Domain Relevance''' | Does this address the specific topic? |
| '''Source Quality''' | Who produced this? What is their track record? |
| '''Methodology''' | Is the approach sound? Can it be replicated? |
| '''Bias Check''' | Who funded this? What conflicts exist? |
| '''Currency''' | Is this current? Has it been superseded? |
| '''Utility''' | Can this be applied? Does it enable action? |

=== Domain Relevance ===

Evidence must be evaluated for its relevance to the specific domain and question at hand. Technical documentation may be highly relevant for implementation questions but irrelevant for theoretical foundations. Domain relevance requires understanding the scope and boundaries of the evidentiary claim.

=== Source Quality ===

Source assessment examines the producer's expertise, track record, and institutional context. Quality indicators include peer review processes, editorial standards, transparency of methods, and historical reliability. However, source quality must be balanced against the context-dependency principle—even reputable sources can produce flawed evidence.

=== Methodology ===

Methodological soundness involves evaluating whether the evidence was produced through appropriate procedures, whether those procedures can be replicated, and whether the methods match the research questions. Methodological transparency is essential for critical assessment.

=== Bias Check ===

Bias assessment examines potential conflicts of interest, funding sources, institutional pressures, and ideological commitments that might influence evidence production. This dimension requires examining not just declared interests but also structural biases embedded in research practices.

=== Currency ===

Evidence currency considers whether the information remains current or has been superseded by more recent findings. Currency is particularly important in rapidly evolving fields where knowledge obsolescence is high.

=== Utility ===

Evidence utility evaluates whether the information can be practically applied and whether it enables effective action. Practical utility is distinct from theoretical validity—evidence may be sound but useless for practical purposes.

----
== Evidence Types ==

These categories describe evidence without ranking:

=== Empirical ===

'' Experimental data
'' Observational studies
'' Measurements and recordings
'' Field observations
'' Sensor data

Empirical evidence derives from direct observation or experimentation. Its value depends on measurement validity, sampling adequacy, and control for confounding variables.

=== Analytical ===

'' Mathematical proofs
'' Logical deductions
'' Model outputs
'' Simulation results
'' Formal derivations

Analytical evidence derives from formal reasoning and mathematical demonstration. Its validity depends on the soundness of the underlying formal system and the correctness of the derivation.

=== Documentary ===

'' Primary sources
'' Technical documentation
'' Historical records
'' Archival materials
'' Original manuscripts

Documentary evidence provides direct access to historical or technical information. Its evaluation requires authentication, provenance verification, and contextual interpretation.

=== Experiential ===

'' Practitioner knowledge
'' Case studies
'' Phenomenological accounts
'' Expert testimony
'' Tacit knowledge

Experiential evidence captures knowledge embedded in practice and experience. While often undervalued in formal hierarchies, practitioner knowledge can provide crucial insights unavailable through other methods (Collins & Evans, 2007).

=== Distributed ===

'' Community consensus (not truth, but coordination)
'' Network-verified data
'' Multi-party attestations
'' Blockchain records
'' Distributed ledger entries

Distributed evidence leverages network effects and multi-party validation. Its strength lies in the difficulty of coordinated manipulation rather than individual source reliability.

----
== Assessment Process ==

# '''Identify the question''': Clarify what is being asked and what would count as evidence
# '''Gather relevant evidence''': Collect potentially relevant sources across evidence types
# '''Evaluate by dimensions''': Apply the six evaluation dimensions systematically
# '''Mark uncertainty''': Explicitly identify gaps, conflicts, and limitations
# '''Document provenance''': Record sources, methods, and assessment rationale

----
== Uncertainty Marking ==

Use markers when:
'' Evidence is preliminary
'' Claims are speculative
'' Sources are contested
'' Context is unclear

Uncertainty marking serves epistemic transparency by making the limits of current knowledge explicit. This practice aligns with the error-statistical approach (Mayo, 1996) and promotes responsible knowledge communication.

----
== Theoretical Foundations ==

The BITwiki Evidence Framework draws upon:

# '''Philosophy of Science''': Understanding how evidence relates to theory (Longino, 1990; Kuhn, 1962)
# '''Social Epistemology''': Recognizing knowledge as socially produced (Goldman, 1999)
# '''Evidence-Based Practice''': Systematic approaches to evidence evaluation (Sackett et al., 1996)
# '''Critical Information Studies''': Examining power and bias in information systems (Fallis, 2008)

----
== References ==

# Longino, H. E. (1990). ''Science as Social Knowledge''. Princeton University Press.
# Douglas, H. (2009). ''Science, Policy, and the Value-Free Ideal''. University of Pittsburgh Press.
# Sackett, D. L., et al. (1996). Evidence based medicine: What it is and what it isn't. ''BMJ'', 312(7023), 71-72.
# Fallis, D. (2008). Toward an epistemology of Wikipedia. ''JASIST'', 59(1), 98-109.
# Howick, J. (2011). ''The Philosophy of Evidence-Based Medicine''. Wiley-Blackwell.
# Collins, H. M., & Evans, R. (2007). ''Rethinking Expertise''. University of Chicago Press.
# Mayo, D. G. (1996). ''Error and the Growth of Experimental Knowledge''. University of Chicago Press.
# Kuhn, T. S. (1962). ''The Structure of Scientific Revolutions''. University of Chicago Press.
# Goldman, A. I. (1999). ''Knowledge in a Social World''. Oxford University Press.
# Cartwright, N. (2007). ''Hunting Causes and Using Them''. Cambridge University Press.
# Stegenga, J. (2018). ''Care and Cure: An Introduction to Philosophy of Medicine''. University of Chicago Press.
# Worrall, J. (2002). What evidence in evidence-based medicine? ''Philosophy of Science'', 69(3), S316-S330.

----
